narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'arrogance' typed as a disposition (D102 type=disposition), a settled inner posture rather than a single act. Its sense (D101) is 'arrogant hot pursuit': self-exaltation that does not stay interior but discharges as a chase. No source is recorded (D103 present:false) - the passage does not trace where the arrogance comes from; it is presented as the given condition of 'the wicked'. The seat (D104) is 'none': this pride is not lodged in a named organ or faculty, it is a whole-person stance. The bearer (D105) is the wicked (inferred); the operation (D106) is the interior turned outward - 'in arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor', pride expressed as predatory chase. The target (D107) reads back as the arrogance itself / the poor who are hunted; manner (D108) is 'none' - no modality is specified beyond the hot pursuit. Intensity, specifier and effect are all absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false): the verse marks no degree, no further qualifier, and does not yet record the outcome of the hunt - the consequence is left open. The coupling (D112) is 'arrogant-pursuit': pride and the hunting of the weak are welded into one movement, not two. Prohibition is absent (D113 present:false) - this is described, not forbidden here. The discovery (D114) fixes the finding: the interior driving the hunt is pride, self-exaltation converted into the chase of the weak. Role (D115) is characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state - it is read as a state of the inner being, its arena being the poor it pursues. Read on the inner-being lens, arrogance here is not mere self-regard but an engine: the swollen self reaches out to prey.
narratives.story: The psalm opens with a man so full of himself that his pride cannot sit still - it turns into a hunt. Puffed up, he chases down the poor and weak like quarry. The poem never says what made him this way; his arrogance is simply there, the whole set of the man rather than something in one corner of him. Pride and predation have fused into a single motion: to be this proud is to prey. The verse stops before telling us how the hunt ends, leaving the outcome hanging - it shows us the swollen self reaching out to seize the helpless, and lets that stand.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'boast' (halal) typed as a disposition (D102 type=disposition) - here a habitual bent of the self, not an isolated speech-act. The sense (D101) is 'boasts of his soul's desire': the vaunting is of one's own cravings. No source is recorded (D103 present:false) - the boasting is not derived from anything; it stands as the native reflex of the wicked. Seat (D104) is 'none' - not organ-located; it is the whole man's stance. Bearer (D105) is the wicked (inferred); the operation (D106) is the full movement - 'the wicked boasts of the cravings of his soul, and the greedy man curses and renounces the LORD'. Target (D107) is 'self-glorying-greed': the boast aims at nothing outside the self; it circles its own appetite. Manner (D108) is 'none' - unqualified. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false): no degree, no qualifier, and the consequence of the boast is not recorded here. Coupling (D112) is 'boast-of-desire' - the boasting is bonded to appetite; the two cannot be separated. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114) states the finding: the interior parades its own appetites as its glory, greed become a creed that dismisses God. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. On the inner-being lens this is pride's speech-face: the self makes its wants its boast and, in the same breath, renounces the LORD - self-glory and God-denial are one interior act.
narratives.story: Here the same wicked man opens his mouth, and what comes out is bragging about the things he craves. He is proud of his own appetite, glorying in his greed as if it were something to celebrate. In the same breath he curses and turns his back on God - the two go together, so that praising himself and dismissing God are really one movement of the heart. The poem does not say what his boasting will cost him; it simply shows a man whose desires have become his creed. The outcome is left unsaid; the picture is complete without it.
narratives.variation_note: Of the five 'boast' (halal) readings this is the only one typed as a settled disposition aimed at 'self-glorying-greed' with God actively renounced; #2 (Psa 44:8) is boasting IN God, #3 (Psa 49:6) in riches, #4 (Psa 52:1) in evil, #5 (Psa 97:7) in idols. This #1 is the appetite-boast - the self glorying in its own cravings, the most inward and God-defiant of the set.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'arrogantly' typed as a disposition (D102 type=disposition). Its sense (D101) is 'enemies closed to pity, arrogant': the arrogance is bound to a shut-off compassion. Source is absent (D103 present:false) - the passage does not say what produced this hardness; it is simply the enemies' condition. Seat (D104) is 'none' - though v10 speaks of hearts closing, the analysis records no organ-seat for the arrogance itself; it is a whole-person disposition. Bearer (D105) is the enemies (inferred); the operation (D106) is a compound movement - 'the enemies close their hearts to pity and speak arrogantly, tracking the self down like a lion eager to tear'. Target (D107) is 'merciless-arrogance'; manner (D108) is 'none' - unqualified. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false): no degree marked, no qualifier, and the outcome (whether the hunt succeeds) is not recorded. Coupling (D112) is 'closed-and-arrogant': pitilessness and arrogant speech are welded together - the mouth's pride and the heart's closure are one thing. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the enemies' interior is shut against mercy and swollen with arrogance, a pitilessness that hunts. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. On the inner-being lens the finding is that arrogance and mercilessness co-occur as a single inner condition: the self so exalted that it feels no pity, its pride audible in the mouth while the heart is barred - and that state reaches outward to hunt the psalmist like a lion.
narratives.story: The psalmist's enemies have hearts bolted shut against pity, and out of those closed hearts comes proud, swaggering talk. The two belong together: their mouths brag because their hearts feel nothing. This pride is not a small flaw tucked away somewhere; it is the whole set of the men, who stalk the psalmist like a hungry lion ready to tear. The poem does not explain how they got so hard, nor does it tell us whether the hunt succeeds - it simply shows arrogance and cruelty as one and the same inner state, a self so swollen it has no room left for mercy.

narratives.narrative: This reading is distinctive within the family: 'presumptuous' is typed not as disposition or action but as volition (D102 type=volition) - a matter of the will. Its sense (D101) is 'kept from presumptuous sin'. Uniquely, the bearer (D105) is the psalmist himself (inferred), not the wicked: the arrogance-word appears from the inside, as a danger the speaker fears in his own interior. Source is absent (D103 present:false) - the passage does not name where presumptuous sin arises. Seat (D104) is 'none' - not organ-located. The operation (D106) is a plea: 'the self asks to be kept from presumptuous sins and not let them have dominion - guarding against willful, ruling sin'. Target (D107) is 'guarding-against-dominion'; manner (D108) 'none'. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false): no degree, no qualifier, and the outcome of the plea is not recorded within the span. Coupling (D112) is 'keep-from-presumption'. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false) - notably, though the sin is deprecated, no formal prohibition is tagged; the guarding is carried as petition, not command. The discovery (D114) sharpens it: distinct from hidden faults, this is the deliberate sin the interior fears could master it; the plea is against being ruled. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. On the inner-being lens this is the family's reflexive pole - presumption (defiant, high-handed sin) seen not in an enemy but as a possible tyrant over the speaker's own soul, so that the movement is a will asking to be kept from a pride that would seize dominion over it.
narratives.story: Here the proud, defiant sin is not out in an enemy - it is a threat the psalmist fears inside himself. He prays to be kept from the bold, willful wrongs that he knows could take him over and rule him. He treats these differently from the small hidden mistakes he cannot even see: presumptuous sin is the deliberate, high-handed kind, and his dread is that it might become his master. The prayer is a matter of the will - a man asking to be guarded before such pride ever takes the throne of his heart. The poem leaves the answer to the prayer unspoken, resting simply in the asking.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'taunt / reproach' (charaph) typed as an action (D102 type=action) - a deed done to the speaker, not a standing state. Sense (D101): 'taunt / reproach (charaph)'. Source is absent (D103 present:false) - no cause is given for the adversaries' scorn. Seat (D104) is 'none' - not organ-located. Bearer (D105) is the adversaries (inferred); the operation (D106) is simply 'taunt'; the target (D107) is David, the speaker himself. Distinctively, this taunt carries a manner (D108): 'like a deadly wound in the bones' (inferred) - the reproach is felt as bodily, mortal injury, not mere words. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false): no numeric degree, no qualifier, and the resulting inner collapse, though present in the surrounding lament, is not tagged as an effect here. Coupling (D112) is 'none' - this taunt is not welded to another act; it stands alone. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the reproach wounds like a mortal blow to the bones, the foes' 'Where is your God?' assaulting the very ground of faith. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state - though the taunt comes from outside, it registers as an inner-being wound. On the inner-being lens the finding is that hostile mockery is not experienced merely as insult but as an attack on faith itself: the jeer 'Where is your God?' penetrates to the bones, so the arena of the taunt is the sufferer's confidence in God.
narratives.story: The psalmist's enemies jeer at him all day long, and their favourite taunt is a question: 'Where is your God?' It is not just an insult he can shrug off - he feels it like a killing blow deep in his bones. The poem does not say why they hate him; the mockery is simply there, aimed straight at him. And the sting is not to his reputation but to his faith: the jeer is designed to make him doubt that God is there at all. The words come from outside, but the wound lands deep inside, on the very thing that holds him up.
narratives.variation_note: Of the four 'taunt' (charaph) readings this one alone carries a manner - the reproach felt 'like a deadly wound in the bones' - and its whole force is the faith-assault 'Where is your God?'; #2 (Psa 55:12) is the endurable taunt of a mere enemy contrasted with a friend's betrayal, #3 (Psa 102:8) is the sufferer taunted all day as a passive state, #4 (Psa 119:42) is the taunter answered by the psalmist's trust. This #1 is the taunt as bodily, faith-piercing wound.

narratives.narrative: This is the family's counter-instance: 'boast / glory' (halal) typed as an action (D102 type=action), but here directed rightly. Sense (D101): 'boast / glory (halal)'. Uniquely for a boast in this set, a source is recorded (D103, pair, span): the boasting is 'grounded in God's past saving deeds (v7)' - it is not self-generated pride but a response to what God has done. Seat (D104) is 'none' - not organ-located. Bearer (D105) is the nation (inferred); operation (D106) 'boast / glory'; and the target (D107) is 'in God' - the vaunting aims away from the self, toward God. Manner (D108) is 'continually' (inferred): habitual, unceasing. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false): no degree, no qualifier, no tagged outcome. Coupling (D112) is a pair: 'paired with giving thanks' - the boast is welded to thanksgiving, not to appetite or evil. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the nation's habitual glorying in God, grounded in his past deeds, the confidence now tested by rejection. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) external:god - alone among the readings here, the locus is God himself, not an inner state. On the inner-being lens the finding is that the very act (halal) that elsewhere in this family is pride's speech is here redeemed: the same movement of glorying, when its source is God's deeds and its target is God, becomes praise - the interior directed outward and upward rather than curved on itself. That this confident boast is set against v9's rejection is the tension the passage holds.
narratives.story: Here the very same act of boasting appears, but turned the right way round. The nation glories 'in God' - not in itself - and it does so all the time, boasting bound up with thanksgiving. This bragging has a real foundation: it rests on the rescues God worked for their fathers, driving out nations and saving them. So the same glorying that elsewhere is arrogance becomes, when it points to God, simply praise. The poignancy is that they say this even as they feel rejected - their confident boast in God stands against the sense that God has turned away, and they hold both together.
narratives.variation_note: This is the only 'boast' (halal) reading whose target is 'in God' and whose locus is external:god, and the only one with a recorded source (God's past deeds) and a positive coupling (thanksgiving). Against #1 (self/greed), #3 (riches), #4 (evil), #5 (idols), #2 shows the identical verb redeemed: the difference in TARGET and SOURCE flips the same movement from pride to praise - decisive evidence that halal's meaning is set by what it is boasted in, not by the act itself.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'reproach / taunt' (cherpah) typed not as an action but as a status (D102 type=status) - a condition the sufferer is put into, not a deed he does. Sense (D101): 'reproach / taunt (cherpah)'. Source is absent (D103 present:false) - no cause named for the disgrace. Seat (D104) is 'none' - not organ-located. Bearer (D105) is the nation, 'made a taunt' (inferred) - the people are the object, reduced to a byword. Distinctively, the operation (D106) is 'none' (resolution none): the nation performs no act; it is acted upon - a striking silence where in most readings an operation is present. Likewise the target (D107) is 'none': there is no one the nation taunts, because the nation IS the taunt. Manner (D108) is a pair: 'derision and scorn of neighbours' - the disgrace is qualified by the surrounding peoples' contempt. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false). Coupling (D112) is 'none'. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the nation reduced to an object of reproach, the once-boasting people derided and scorned by those around. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. On the inner-being lens the finding is the underside of #2 (Psa 44:8): the people who boasted in God are now themselves made a public shame. The empty operation and empty target are the point - this taunt is a passive humiliation, a state of being scorned, the interior collapse of a people whose glory has become disgrace.
narratives.story: The nation that once boasted proudly in God is now the joke of the neighbourhood. God has, as it were, sold them off cheap, and the surrounding peoples sneer and scorn them. Here the people do nothing - they are not the ones mocking; they are the ones mocked, turned into a byword. That is the whole weight of it: they have become a thing others laugh at. The same people who gloried in God a few lines earlier now sit in disgrace, their proud confidence turned inside out into public shame.
narratives.variation_note: This is the family's only H2781 (cherpah) reading typed as a status with an empty operation and empty target - the sufferer is the taunt, not the taunter. It is the deliberate inverse of the same passage's #2 (Psa 44:8) boast in God: proud glorying and public disgrace bracket one psalm, and the reversal is itself the finding.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'boast' (halal) typed as an action (D102 type=action). Sense (D101): 'boast (halal)'. Source absent (D103 present:false) - the passage does not derive the boasting from a prior cause. Seat (D104) 'none' - not organ-located. Bearer (D105) is the rich (inferred); operation (D106) 'boast'; target (D107) is 'the abundance of their riches' - the vaunting aims at wealth. Manner (D108) 'none'. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false): no degree, no qualifier, and the outcome (death exposing the folly) belongs to the wider passage but is not tagged here. Coupling (D112) is a pair: 'paired with trusting in wealth' - the boast is welded to trust; to brag of riches is to lean on them. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the fool's self-glory in riches, the vaunting that death exposes as folly. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. On the inner-being lens the finding is that this boast is misplaced trust made audible: the interior rests its security on wealth and then broadcasts it, so that pride and trust are the same motion pointed at a thing that cannot ransom a life. Against the family's God-directed boast (#2), here the target is riches; the same act curves onto possessions rather than God.
narratives.story: These are people who trust their money and then brag about how much of it they have. Their boasting and their trusting are the same thing: they lean on their wealth and can't help showing it off. But the poem sets this against a hard fact - no amount of riches can buy anyone out of death. The bragging that feels so solid is really folly, and death will expose it. Where the good kind of boasting points to God, this one points to a bank balance that cannot save its owner.
narratives.variation_note: Among the five 'boast' (halal) readings this one alone targets 'the abundance of riches' and is coupled to 'trusting in wealth' - pride as misplaced security. It differs from #2 (boast in God), #1 (in one's own greed), #4 (in evil) and #5 (in idols): here the object is wealth, and the finding is that boasting and trusting fuse, both aimed at what death nullifies.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'boast / make a show' (halal) typed as an action (D102 type=action), here 'boast in evil'. Sense (D101): 'boast / make a show (halal - boast in evil)'. Distinctively, a source is recorded (D103, pair, span): the boast is 'set against God's steadfast love that endures continually (v1)' - the passage frames the vaunting by contrast with God's enduring chesed. Seat (D104) 'none' - not organ-located. Bearer (D105) is the tyrant, Doeg / the mighty man (inferred); operation (D106) 'boast / glory'; and the target (D107) is a pair: 'in evil' - the mighty man glories precisely in wickedness. Manner (D108) is 'all the day long' (inferred): relentless. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false). Coupling (D112) is 'none' - the boast is not welded to a further act here; it stands as its own perversion. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the strongman's self-glorying in wickedness, halal (the praise-verb) perverted into boasting of harm, futile against God's steadfast love that 'endures all the day'. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. On the inner-being lens the finding is the darkest turn of halal in this family: not boasting in God, or riches, or self, but in evil itself - the interior taking pride in its capacity to do harm, and doing so continually, while the very love it defies simply endures. The source-contrast is the passage's verdict: the tyrant's ceaseless boast is set against, and dwarfed by, God's ceaseless love.
narratives.story: A powerful man stands there bragging - not about wealth or status, but about the evil he can do. He glories in his own capacity for harm, and he keeps it up all day long. The poem sets his endless boasting against something that also lasts all day: God's steadfast love. That contrast is the whole point. His pride in wickedness looks strong, but it is empty and doomed next to a love that simply goes on enduring. This is bragging at its most twisted - a heart that takes pride in the damage it can inflict.
narratives.variation_note: This is the only 'boast' (halal) reading whose target is 'in evil' and whose manner is 'all the day long', explicitly framed against God's enduring steadfast love. Set beside #2 (in God), #1 (in greed), #3 (in riches), #5 (in idols), #4 is halal at its most perverse - the praise-verb turned to glorying in harm - and the source-contrast (v1) is what marks its futility.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'laugh / deride' (sachaq) typed as an action (D102 type=action). Sense (D101): 'laugh / deride (sachaq - laugh at him)'. Source absent (D103 present:false) - no prior cause named for the laughter beyond what the passage shows. Seat (D104) 'none' - not organ-located. Distinctively, the bearer (D105) is 'the righteous' (inferred), not the wicked - here derision is on the just side. Operation (D106) 'laugh / deride'; target (D107) 'at the fallen tyrant'; manner (D108) 'in derision' (inferred). Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false). Coupling (D112) is a pair: 'the response after seeing and fearing' - the laughter is welded to a prior seeing-and-fearing (v6), so it is not careless mockery but reverent recognition turned to scorn of the fallen. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the righteous' derision at the strongman brought to nothing - not cruelty but the vindication of justice ('See the man who would not make God his refuge!'). Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) external:person - the laughter is directed at another person, the fallen tyrant. On the inner-being lens the finding is that scornful laughter is morally ambivalent within this family: the same derision that from the wicked (Psa 73:8; 102:8) is malice is, from the righteous who first see and fear, an act of vindicated justice. The coupling to fear is decisive - this laugh is grounded in awe of God's judgment, not in self-exaltation.
narratives.story: When God finally breaks down the boastful tyrant, the righteous watch it happen - and first they are struck with awe, then they laugh. Their laughter is not cruelty for its own sake; it grows out of that awe. They point at the fallen strongman and say, in effect, 'Look at the man who would not make God his refuge, but trusted his riches instead.' It is the laugh of justice being proved right. The same scornful laughter that is malice in wicked mouths becomes, here, the relief of people who have seen God set things straight.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'magnify oneself / deal insolently' (gadal) typed as an action (D102 type=action). Sense (D101): 'magnify oneself / deal insolently (gadal)'. Source absent (D103 present:false). Seat (D104) 'none' - not organ-located. Bearer (D105) is distinctive: 'the hypothetical open hater' (inferred) - the insolence belongs to an imagined open enemy, not the actual betrayer. Operation (D106) 'magnify himself / behave arrogantly'; target (D107) 'against the psalmist'; manner (D108) 'none'. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false). Coupling (D112) is a pair: 'the act of the open adversary' - the insolence is welded to the figure of the overt foe, the one from whom escape is possible. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the open arrogance one could avoid - gadal, the enemy's overt self-exalting, from which escape is possible, unlike the hidden dagger of a friend. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) external:person. On the inner-being lens the finding hinges on the hypothetical bearer: the psalmist reasons that an openly insolent enemy would be bearable because one can hide from him; the pain is that the arrogance he actually suffers comes cloaked as friendship. So this reading of self-magnifying pride functions by contrast - overt arrogance is the tolerable evil against which the covert betrayal is measured.
narratives.story: The psalmist imagines a straightforwardly arrogant enemy - the kind who puffs himself up and openly comes at you. If it were only that, he says, he could cope; you can hide from an enemy you can see. But that is not his real trouble. His actual pain comes from someone close, a friend who betrayed him, whose arrogance was hidden behind warm words. So he holds up the picture of the open, insolent foe precisely to say: that would have been the easy version. Plain pride you can dodge; it is the concealed kind, from a friend, that truly wounds.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'taunt / reproach' (charaph) typed as an action (D102 type=action). Sense (D101): 'taunt / reproach (charaph - it is not an enemy who taunts)'. Source absent (D103 present:false). Seat (D104) 'none' - not organ-located. Distinctively, the bearer (D105) is 'a hypothetical enemy (not the betrayer)' (inferred): as with the paired gadal reading, the taunt is imagined, framed to sharpen a contrast. Operation (D106) 'taunt / reproach'; target (D107) 'the psalmist'; manner (D108) 'none'. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false). Coupling (D112) is a pair: 'the reproach he could have borne' - the taunt is welded to the idea of endurability. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the reproach that from a known foe would be endurable - the pain is precisely that it comes from a friend, not an enemy. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) external:person. On the inner-being lens the finding is that the taunt-word is used here counterfactually: a taunt from an enemy would be survivable ('then I could bear it'). The interior force is not the mockery itself but its source - betrayal by an intimate. So this reading measures pain by relationship: the same reproach that is bearable from a foe is unbearable from a friend, and that is the wound the passage names.
narratives.story: The psalmist says something surprising: if the person mocking him were an enemy, he could take it. Insults from a known foe are survivable - you expect them. But that is not what has happened to him. The one tearing him down is a close friend, a companion he once walked with and shared secrets with. So he holds up the picture of an enemy's taunt only to say how much worse his own case is. The words themselves might have been bearable; what makes them cut so deep is who they came from.
narratives.variation_note: This 'taunt' (charaph) reading is counterfactual - a taunt from a hypothetical enemy, 'which I could bear', set against a friend's betrayal. It differs from #1 (Psa 42:10, the faith-piercing 'Where is your God?'), #3 (Psa 102:8, the sufferer taunted all day) and #4 (Psa 119:42, the taunter answered by trust): here the taunt's force lies not in its content but in the relationship it exposes - pain is measured by the nearness of the one who inflicts it.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'pride / arrogance' (gaon) typed as a status (D102 type=status) - a standing condition of the enemies. Sense (D101): 'pride / arrogance (gaon - trapped in their pride)'. Distinctively, a source is recorded (D103, pair, span): the pride is that 'which God's wrath will consume (v13)' - the passage links the pride forward to its judgment. Seat (D104) 'none' - not organ-located. Bearer (D105) is the enemies (inferred); the operation (D106) is striking - 'trap them (their pride the snare)' (inferred): the pride functions as the very net in which the proud are caught. Target (D107) 'none'; manner (D108) 'none'. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (D109/D110/D111 present:false): the outcome (being consumed) is framed as source/prayer, not tagged as effect. Coupling (D112) is a pair: 'the sin of their mouths and cursing' - the pride is welded to their cursing speech; their arrogant words are the substance of the snare. Prohibition absent (D113 present:false). The discovery (D114): the arrogance that becomes the snare - so that their own pride ensnares them, caught by the very loftiness of their cursing speech, to be consumed in God's wrath. Role (D115) characteristic; locus (D116) internal:ib-state. On the inner-being lens the finding is that pride here is self-defeating: the interior state does not merely provoke judgment but is itself the trap that springs on its bearer. The proud mouth's cursing is both the sin and the snare - pride as an inner condition that turns and catches the one who holds it.
narratives.story: The psalmist prays that his enemies would be caught in their own pride. Their arrogance is not just an attitude; it becomes the very trap that snares them. What springs the trap is their own mouths - the cursing and lies they pour out. Their high, boastful speech is both the crime and the snare that catches them by the ankle. And the poem points ahead to where it all leads: God's anger will burn them up. Pride, here, is a thing that turns on the proud, so that the very loftiness they flaunt is what brings them down.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'arrogant / boastful' (halal) typed here as a status (D102 type=status) - a standing description of the wicked, not an act they perform. Their arrogance is not a private feeling tucked away inside; it is on open display, flaunted like an ornament. What should be a shameful thing they treat as decoration. This is not light-hearted teasing; it is the overflow of hearts so untroubled and swollen that they hold everyone in scorn. Their pride has become a sneer that also menaces, contempt that is ready to do damage.

Pride here is not just a feeling but a stance: a rigid neck that will not bend, and a mouth that speaks up against heaven. And the poem's point is that the Judge will bring that stiff neck low.

It is a bold, bitter picture: God's enemies openly deriding him, and the psalmist laying that insult before God as part of his cry for help.

These are arrogant people who trample God's own people, crushing the weak and the helpless. Their pride is not idle; it is turned against others, and it has earned a reckoning. It is pride that has become a flood of talk - a torrent of bragging. Where the poem first pictured them as proud oppressors deserving judgment, here it lets us hear them: a stream of arrogant speech spilling out of evildoers who cannot stop exalting themselves. narratives.story: These are people who brag about their idols - carved images that can do nothing at all. They glory in them, bound up with bowing down to worship them. But the poem is blunt: such boasting is pride poured into emptiness. Where boasting in God is praise with a real foundation, boasting in idols is glorying in nothing, and it ends in shame. All who trust in worthless images are put to shame when the true God appears. It is the emptiest kind of pride - a heart proudly committed to what has no power to help it.

God rebukes them; they are under his curse for wandering off the path. This same arrogant enemy keeps turning up throughout the psalm, deriding, slandering and pressing on the psalmist again and again. But here the emphasis falls on their defection: their pride is a refusal to follow God's word, and it is God himself, not the psalmist, who answers it with rebuke. They are the recurring proud foes who dog the whole poem, defined by their turning away from the law.

The derision lands, but it changes nothing - his faithfulness holds.

The afflicted have had more than enough of this contempt; they are full to the brim with it. So they lift their eyes to God, the way a servant watches a master's hand, waiting for mercy. The picture sets two things side by side: proud people at ease pouring contempt downward, and humbled people looking upward for help. Pride here is the sneer of the secure at the suffering.

narratives.story: This psalm says something quietly devastating about pride. Though God is high above all, he pays close attention to the lowly and humble - he draws near to them. But the haughty, the proud, he knows only from a distance. Their self-importance does not impress him closer; it pushes him further away. The two are set side by side: the humble get God's nearness, the proud get his distance. It is not so much that pride is punished as that it simply keeps God at arm's length. The higher a person lifts himself, the farther off God stands.

narratives.story: The psalmist prays for protection from arrogant men, but their arrogance takes a surprising form. It is not loud bragging - it is quiet and sneaky. These proud men set hidden traps, spreading nets and laying snares along the path where he walks, hoping to catch him unawares. Their pride works by ambush, not open attack. It is a calculating kind of arrogance that hides its hand and waits. So the psalmist asks God to keep him from these concealed snares, aware that pride can be all the more dangerous when it stops shouting and starts scheming in secret.
